Where it began

Keshav Maharaj was born in Durban on 7 February 1990. Cricket ran in the family: his father, Athmanand, kept wicket for KwaZulu-Natal. Keshav was quick to follow, making his first-class debut for KwaZulu-Natal at 16 in the 2006–07 season. He learned his trade in the domestic game with the Dolphins, and with spells in English club and league cricket, at Cuckfield and as the professional at Nelson. In one match for the Dolphins in 2016–17 he made 72 and then took 13 wickets, which is about as busy as one man can be in a single game.

The player

He made his Test debut at Perth on 3 November 2016, taking three wickets, and became the first specialist spinner to make a Test debut on that ground. By November 2026 he had played 63 Tests and taken 220 wickets at 29.55, with 12 five-wicket innings and one ten-wicket match, and he ranked 77th among all Test bowlers for wickets.

His best day came in July 2018, when he took 9 for 129 against Sri Lanka. No visiting bowler had ever done better in a Test innings in Sri Lanka, and among South Africans only Hugh Tayfield had returned better figures. In 2021 in the West Indies he took a Test hat-trick, only the second by a South African, and the first since Geoff Griffin managed one in 1960. He was part of the side that won the World Test Championship for 2023–2025, and when he led South Africa in a Test, they won it.

What made him special

Spinners in South Africa often spend their careers waiting for the pitch to help. Maharaj made himself the man who did the job anyway: accurate, tireless and clever with his drift, able to hold an end while the fast bowlers rested and to take wickets when the surface finally turned. He was a useful batter too, with six Test fifties and a best of 84.

He never made a Test hundred, and 1,369 runs at 15.56 suggests the batting stayed a sideline. Even so, anyone who has seen him dig in with the tail knows he treated every run as a personal project.

Away from the middle

In 2017 Cricket South Africa named him International Newcomer of the Year. He became a white-ball cricketer of note too: he captained South Africa on his Twenty20 international debut and took a wicket with his very first ball, and at the 2023 World Cup in India he was among the most economical bowlers of the tournament. He played county cricket for Lancashire and Yorkshire, taking 38 wickets at 18.92 for Yorkshire in 2019, and captained sides in the SA20.

And finally

A wicket with your first ball in a format, as captain, on debut, is the kind of thing most cricketers would not dare to dream up. Maharaj simply did it, and then went back to bowling the next one.
